name: Hair stem cell mesotherapy

card.summary: Scalp micro-injections of stem-cell-derived or similar preparations, marketed to support hair growth and thicken thinning hair.
card.note: Preparations vary and regulators do not oversee mixtures; infection risk depends on the provider.

quick.overview:
Hair stem cell mesotherapy refers to clinic treatments in which preparations marketed as stem-cell based are injected into the scalp in many tiny injections. The aim is to stimulate follicles and thicken hair in people with thinning.

The appearance goal is denser-looking hair on the scalp. Related scalp injection treatments such as platelet-rich plasma have been studied for pattern hair loss, while this specific form lacks dedicated trials.
quick.how: Treatment is done at clinics, often as a series of sessions followed by maintenance, as with PRP protocols that call for at least three monthly sessions then maintenance every 3-6 months.[3] Users often combine it with finasteride or minoxidil, as hair clinics commonly do.
quick.risks: Mesotherapy injections are not directly policed by the FDA in the US, and their contents are often not disclosed.[1] Reported problems with mesotherapy generally include inflammation, abscesses and infection.[1] A 2024 case of HIV after PRP-microneedling at an unlicensed spa illustrates how provider hygiene matters.[3]

lead: Mesotherapy is a technique in which practitioners inject drugs, enzymes, hormones, plant extracts, vitamins or hyaluronic acid into the middle layers of the skin; it was developed by Michel Pistor in France and recognised by France's Académie Nationale de Médecine as a specialty in 1987.[1] Hair stem cell mesotherapy applies the approach to the scalp using preparations marketed as stem-cell based.

The concept is that growth factors and signalling molecules delivered near follicles could stimulate hair growth. Platelet-rich plasma, a related scalp injection, has been studied for androgenetic alopecia and alopecia areata, and one review reported improved hair density and thickness in men and women.[3]

Wikipedia's mesotherapy article states the technique has no proven clinical efficacy, and a UT Southwestern plastic surgeon is quoted saying there is no data it works; dermatology groups have called for more research.[1]

chain: Injected preparation delivers growth signals near follicles
angle.text: Clinics market scalp injections as a way to thicken thinning hair. The related PRP literature reports density gains in some reviews, but the stem-cell version has little dedicated research.

infobox: Injected mixtures not directly policed by FDA

paras: Mesotherapy delivers substances into the skin through small injections.[1] Hair versions target the scalp; the injected material is described by providers as containing stem cell derived factors, though contents vary and are often not disclosed.[1]

PRP is regulated as a clinical use rather than a product and is off-label for hair loss; its adverse effects are generally low in trials.[3] Wikipedia's article does not clearly rate its hair-loss studies and describes evidence for PRP overall as mixed.[3]

Reported mesotherapy problems include inflammation, abscesses in a group of Australian clients and temporary bruising and pain.[1] Contaminated equipment at an unlicensed spa led to three HIV diagnoses in 2024 after PRP-microneedling.[3]
No studies found on stem cell mesotherapy for hair specifically. Studies of the broader category, such as PRP for hair loss, exist and are summarised above.[3]

timeline.event: France's Académie Nationale de Médecine recognises mesotherapy as a specialty.[1]
